text.author: James P. Cannon and Justice Michael A. Musmanno
text.title: Correspondence between James P. Cannon, Michael A. Musmanno, and Tom O'Connor, 1963
text.summary1: (human1) In letters from 1962-1963, James P. Cannon denies claims by Francis Russel in a book and in the New Republic that he believed and privately stated that Sacco and Vanzetti, who had been executed decades earlier, were guilty, and corresponds with Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justic Michael A. Musmanno, who applauds Cannon and concurs the two were innocent and Russel is unreliable.
text.summary2: (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929; postedited) In a 1962/1963 letter exchange with Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Michael A. Musmanno, James P. Cannon refutes Francis Russell's published claim that he privately admitted thinking Sacco was guilty, asserting he always believed in Sacco and Vanzetti's innocence and criticizing Russell's careless historical methods.
text.summary3: (gpt4o) In a letter to the New Republic, James P. Cannon refutes Francis Russell's claim that he believed Sacco was guilty, affirming his long-held stance on Sacco and Vanzetti's innocence, while Justice Michael A. Musmanno commends Cannon for his clarity and provides further criticism of Russell's historical inaccuracies.
text.summary4: (Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct) James P. Cannon disputes Francis Russell's claim that he privately admitted Sacco's guilt, stating he has always believed the pair were innocent.
text.summary5: (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) James P. Cannon writes to the New Republic and others to refute Francis Russell's claims about his thoughts on the Sacco and Vanzetti case, providing evidence of his belief in their innocence and disputing Russell's historical inaccuracies.
